(MO-MINLP) is a highly versatile yet difficult computational challenge that frequently arises in real-world applications. To address this, we introduce a novel solution approach that integrates the Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithm based on Decomposition (MOEA/D) with various A* search strategies. This method transforms the original MO-MINLP problems into a sequence of Single-Object Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (SO-MINLP) problems, each featuring a sum of squares objective and a path-finding constraint. This specific objective function guarantees convexity and differentiability, enabling the different NLP solvers tested to function efficiently. Furthermore, leveraging the network structure inherent in these SO-MINLP problems, we apply multiple variants of the A* algorithm alongside Dijkstra's method to address the path-finding component. The resulting framework, termed Multi-Objective A* (MOA*), allows us to generate a set of high-quality feasible solutions for various MO-MINLP instances within significantly reduced runtimes. We validate our approach by solving several standard benchmark problems and modeling a case study involving the optimal design of a water distribution network. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of different A* variants and compare their results against those of ε-constraint and Weighted-Sum methods. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach and its variants are exceptionally well-suited for solving general MO-MINLP problems, achieving superior solution quality and computational efficiency. Finally, the case study results demonstrate that our method can identify a near-optimal Pareto front and generate a near-optimal optimal master plan for the water distribution network design. These outcomes are achieved with an order of magnitude improvement in runtime compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Consequently, our approach holds the potential to deliver real-time solutions for practical applications. In summary, this research delivers two primary contributions: first, the development of the innovative MOA* method, and second, the successful application of this approach to multi-objective problems by using it to solve a multi-objective design problem for a water distribution network. These contributions are expected to offer valuable insights and practical value to researchers and practitioners working on real-world MO-MINLP challenges. By analyzing the lag time between corresponding events recorded by each vessel, we determined the energy flux transport time. Our results indicate that the energy flux transport time (FT) scales linearly with the solar wind's dynamic pressure (Pdyn), following the relation $FT = 0.0014 P^{0.992}_{dyn} + 0.0025$. This linear correlation suggests that the solar wind behaves as a homogeneous medium with constant density. Furthermore, we compared our findings with existing literature and observed that the exponent of the power law describing FT's dependence on Pdyn is approximately 0.5 when calculated from a single spacecraft's data. This discrepancy implies that the exponent for a homogeneous medium is roughly double that of a decreasing density medium. Additionally, the exponent derived from our inter-vessel data (0.992) is approximately 0.5 times the exponent obtained from a single-vessel analysis (1.96). Finally, we investigated FT in the outer heliosphere (r > 1 AU) using data from the Ulysses and Ulysses2 missions, finding that the exponent of the power law for energy flux transport time in the outer heliosphere is approximately 0.25. This value is roughly 0.125 times the exponent observed in the inner heliosphere (0.992). These results support the hypothesis that the solar wind is a homogeneous medium and suggest that the energy flux transport time in the inner heliosphere is approximately four times that in the outer heliosphere. The observed FT values in the outer heliosphere align with the time intervals between recurrent events caused by solar wind structures in the inner heliosphere. This consistency further validates the assumption that the solar wind is homogeneous and that the energy flux transport time in the inner heliosphere is approximately four times that in the outer heliosphere. While supervised approaches have achieved significant success through pre-labeled data, they are constrained by the high cost of annotation and an over-reliance on predefined event types and templates. To address these limitations, recent research has shifted focus to unsupervised or weakly supervised methods, which utilize natural language text or knowledge base templates as supervision signals. This study advances the field of unsupervised EE by introducing a novel model called USTructuredE, which leverages text from structured event sources. Specifically, we transform these sources into text-encoded event structures and employ structured text clustering to identify event types and templates, followed by rule-based event extraction. Our evaluations on the extraction task demonstrate that our model significantly surpasses prior state-of-the-art baselines and existing cluster-based models across multiple metrics, including exact match, F1, and recall on an established dataset. Furthermore, we perform the first comprehensive analysis of structured text properties and their impact on EE performance, as well as a detailed examination of our model's performance relative to text similarity and structured text properties. The findings indicate that text contribution is highly dependent on the text source, with shorter texts and those containing more event arguments yielding superior results. Additionally, our model exhibits robustness against text segmentation and demonstrates strong generalization to previously unseen event types and templates. We demonstrate that the direct image of the curvature of these vector bundles, integrated against a specific positive form derived from the metrics on the fibers, equals the curvature of the flag bundle's curvature, integrated against a corresponding positive form derived from the metrics on the fibers. This result extends the classical theorem by Griffiths and Simpson from projective algebraic varieties to arbitrary complex manifolds. Furthermore, it offers a proof of the second part of Simpson's conjecture for arbitrary complex manifolds and provides an alternative derivation of the first part for projective algebraic varieties. Additionally, we establish that the curvature map is continuous with respect to the $C^0$-topology on the space of Hermitian metrics, integrating a specific formula for the curvature of the induced metrics on flag bundles. This finding extends the work of Zhang and Meng from projective algebraic varieties to complex manifolds and serves as the projective algebraic proof of the second component of Simpson's conjecture. As a corollary, we provide an alternative proof of a theorem by Zhang concerning the continuity of curvature under varying Hermitian metrics on a projective algebraic variety, which was originally established using different methods. This paper also corrects and completes certain arguments in the proof of Zhang's theorem. Finally, we introduce a generalized concept of Griffiths positivity applicable to morphisms of Hermitian holomorphic vector bundles, which extends the definitions of relative and relative total positivity for such morphisms on projective algebraic varieties. We investigate fundamental properties of this new notion and its relationship to the curvature of direct images, thereby generalizing several results by Zhang to the context of Hermitian holomorphic vector bundles on complex manifolds. In this framework, we prove that the curvature of such bundles integrates to positive forms against positive forms derived from the metrics on the fibers, thus generalizing Simpson's conjecture from projective algebraic varieties to Hermitian holomorphic vector bundles on complex manifolds. Relative total positivity for these bundles is also defined and explored within this context. To achieve these findings, we develop new techniques, including a relative version of the logarithmic comparison theorem for connections and novel methods for integrating characteristic classes via the holonomy map. These innovations may prove valuable in future research. Finally, we provide an overview of numerous related topics, such as relative positivity and relative Hodge theory on projective algebraic varieties, to contextualize this work. We present a comprehensive study of clumping in the wind of the well-known X-ray binary Cyg X-1 by analyzing the evolution of spectral features in the 0.02--100 keV range using XMM-Newton data collected between 1997 and 2017. Our findings indicate that the wind density is $1.5 \times 10^{14}$ cm$^{-3}$ at a distance of $1.2 \times 10^{13}$ cm from the star, and this density is independent of the clumping factor. Furthermore, the observed X-ray wind density is roughly an order of magnitude lower than theoretical predictions, a discrepancy that remains constant across all epochs. These results imply that the outflow originates from a region significantly smaller than the critical radius. Finally, the clumping factor remains constant over time, with a value of $f$ = 1.8 $\pm$ 0.1.

This term introduces an additional force that drives the theory toward confinement at low energies while ensuring perturbative stability at high energies. By employing the energy-momentum tensor of the aether field to define an aether four-velocity, the model ensures general covariance despite violating Lorentz symmetry. Using a mean-field approximation, we analyze how this extra force modifies the theory's behavior, results, and solutions. In the absence of non-abelian effects, the solution aligns with the standard aether model's predictions. However, this magnitude is sufficient to produce observable effects in the late universe, such as variations in the speed of light and modifications to the Friedmann equation. Finally, we also examine the implications for the early universe. Our findings suggest that if this additional force were to influence the early universe, it would need to be approximately 100 orders of magnitude stronger than its current value. This could potentially explain the origin of the universe's mass scale and the matter-antimatter asymmetry. By analyzing tidal features in COSMOS-3000 galaxies, we evaluate their morphology and detectability across various wavelengths. Our findings reveal that tidal features are more prominent in the 1.4 GHz radio observations than in optical or near-infrared images, a result that aligns with theoretical models and numerical simulations. These results underscore the critical role of radio wavelengths in studying galaxy interactions and measuring their dynamical masses. We also examine the prospects for using radio surveys to investigate dark matter sub-halos within galaxy pairs. Finally, we conclude that incorporating radio wavelengths is essential for a comprehensive understanding of galaxy interactions and their associated dynamical properties. Large Hadron Collider (LHC) began colliding protons at an unprecedented energy of 13 tera-electron volts (TeV). This study examines the production of the vector meson $\rho^0$ in $\mathrm{p+p}$ collisions at this new energy and compares the findings with data from lower collision energies. Measurements of the transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) spectra for $\rho^0$ mesons are reported across various mean multiplicities, utilizing the forward electromagnetic calorimeter (EMC) and the central tracking system of the ATLAS detector. The analyses cover the ranges $1 < p_{\mathrm{T}} < 10$ GeV/$c$ and $5 < p_{\mathrm{T}} < 100$ GeV/$c$, with corresponding multiplicity intervals of $1 < n_{\mathrm{ch}} < 5$, $5 < n_{\mathrm{ch}} < 10$, and $10 < n_{\mathrm{ch}} < 20$. The results demonstrate that the ATLAS detector accurately reproduces the inclusive $\rho^0$ meson yield and its $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectrum at the 13 TeV LHC energy. Furthermore, the measured multiplicities align with theoretical predictions derived from Monte Carlo event generators. The study also investigates the dependence of $\rho^0$ meson yields on particle density and $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ within the rapidity range $2.4 < y < 4.4$. Additionally, the ratio of $\rho^0$ mesons to charged particles is measured as a function of $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ and particle density. Finally, the analysis explores the relationship between the $\rho^0$ meson yield and the $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectrum of all final-state particles. These results are compared with measurements from other colliders, including RHIC, LHCb, and CMS, which observed a suppression in the $\rho^0$ meson yield relative to $p_{\mathrm{T}}$-independent predictions. A similar suppression is evident in the current data. The study concludes by discussing these results in the context of hadron resonance reconstruction methods and the coalescence model. The data support the hypothesis that this suppression arises from the $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ spectra of the constituent particles. While the oscillations of radioactive elements like cesium provide an exceptionally stable and consistent measure of time, the rate of a perfect clock can still vary when observed from different reference frames due to relative motion or variations in the local gravitational field. In the Global Positioning System (GPS), the primary objective is to determine the precise location of a point in space by calculating the distance from the point to a known location. This is achieved by measuring the time required for radio signals to travel between the two points. Because the transmitted and received signals may be subject to different gravitational potentials and velocities, the time intervals recorded by the receiver and the transmitter can differ. Consequently, the distance is determined by multiplying the measured time interval by the speed of light, assuming the signal propagates at that speed.

To ensure accuracy, the proper time intervals measured by each satellite's onboard atomic clock must be corrected to align with the coordinate time used in the Earth-centered inertial frame. This correction accounts for the time dilation caused by the satellite's orbital speed and its altitude above the Earth's surface. The uncorrected time dilation effects are detailed in the section on the Schwarzschild metric.

After this correction, the coordinate time is used to calculate the proper time experienced by an observer on the Earth's surface, which is essential for determining the observer's location. The final position calculation also incorporates the Earth's rotation and the proper time of the receiver, as explained in the segment on Earth-fixed coordinates.

Furthermore, we establish that under appropriate conditions, a $k$-th order deformation extends to a formal infinite jet, with its obstruction also being related to the adjoint of the $k$-th jet. COVID-19) pandemic has profoundly affected numerous nations, with China serving as the initial epicenter. Although China implemented strict containment measures upon the outbreak, the surge in cases has since shifted to countries that previously enjoyed low infection rates. Consequently, preventing further case growth remains a critical priority for these nations. To address this, researchers have developed various strategies, including the use of machine learning models to forecast infection trends. This study introduces a novel forecasting model utilizing the ARIMA time series algorithm, supported by the Seasonal Trend decomposition using Loess (STL) method. Additionally, an intervention analysis was conducted to assess the impact of China's containment policies on global infection trends. The results indicate that while the proposed model is effective, China's containment efforts had no statistically significant effect on worldwide COVID-19 infections at the 5% significance level, as determined by an F-test. Furthermore, the model's performance was evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), yielding values of 1.01 and 1.15, respectively. These metrics suggest that the model is suitable for short-term forecasting but may be less accurate for longer-term predictions. Finally, the daily projected cases for the subsequent 15 days are provided in the associated supplementary material. experience remains a primary objective in cognitive neuroscience. To address this, we must identify specific brain activity patterns that align with subjective reports of visual perception. This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing neural data using a neural network model of human consciousness. We demonstrate the application of this framework on both simulated and real-world datasets. The approach involves training a deep convolutional neural network to generate reconstructions of images presented to a human observer, with attention directed specifically to the central region of the visual field. Subsequently, we apply this framework to simulated data and to electrocorticographic recordings collected from awake humans while random Gabor stimuli were displayed within a virtual reality environment. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between simulated neural activity and human responses. Furthermore, we successfully localized the representation of stimulus features within the early stages of the neural network, while later stages encoded details regarding attention and awareness. We also illustrate how the curvature of these representations can serve as a biomarker for consciousness. We anticipate that this analysis method will provide valuable insights into consciousness research and facilitate the development of more accurate brain-computer interfaces. The accompanying code repository includes implementations for both simulated and real data. Additionally, we have established an open dataset of electrocorticogram recordings paired with participant responses to gather community feedback and further refine our methodologies. Our results demonstrate that neural signals from primary visual cortex contain sufficient information to reconstruct key features of a stimulus, contingent upon whether the subject attended to and consciously perceived the image. These signals can be decoded using a deep neural network architecture inspired by human visual processing. We show that a recurrent deep neural network can accurately decode both attended and unattended representations of abstract images based on electrocorticogram data from the human visual cortex. This decoding is achieved through a recurrent architecture that incorporates working memory and decision-making mechanisms similar to those in the human brain. The decoding accuracy surpasses that of established machine learning methods. These outcomes offer new insights into the human brain's processing of visual information and suggest that neural activity in the visual cortex can reveal details about attention and awareness. The decoding network generates activation patterns that form readable "maps" of key stimulus features across distinct processing stages. These maps exhibit distinct differences between representations that are attended versus unattended. We demonstrate that curvature can function as a biomarker for consciousness and that neural signals from the visual cortex are capable of encoding important image features. We examine how Jupiter's resonant perturbations influence the asteroid belt and analyze the likelihood of these bodies colliding with Earth. Our findings indicate that assuming a uniform initial spatial distribution for the cluster leads to a high collision rate with Earth, reaching approximately 10^-4 per year. However, if the asteroids were initially distributed according to a Gaussian probability distribution, the collision rate would drop significantly to roughly 10^-6 per year. These results underscore the critical role of initial conditions in assessing impact risks. Furthermore, we observe that Jupiter's resonant perturbations can occasionally excite the orbital inclinations of compact asteroids, thereby substantially increasing their probability of impacting Earth. Finally, we demonstrate that asteroids trapped in the 2:1 Jupiter resonance can be ejected from the solar system over timescales of approximately 10^7 years due to perturbations from Neptune and Uranus. This mechanism may account for the existence of the recently discovered Atira asteroids, which orbit inside Jupiter's orbit. Our analysis suggests that about 10% of Atira asteroids could have originated from the 2:1 Jupiter resonance. These outcomes offer valuable insights into the dynamics of compact asteroid clusters and their potential threats to Earth. Our findings indicate that participants generally have a clear understanding of which measures are most effective, yet they often struggle to estimate the probability of success for each one. Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between a measure's perceived efficacy and its perceived undesirability. Consistent with the burden theory, we observed that perceiving a method as effective does not necessarily mean participants are willing to accept the associated costs, such as social isolation. These results suggest the need for online campaigns that not only explain the effectiveness of preventive actions but also address the uncertainties surrounding them and clarify the costs and benefits to encourage adoption. Furthermore, we found that individuals' perceptions are influenced by their demographic traits, including age, gender, and prior personal experience with COVID-19. Finally, we developed a predictive model using participants' responses to demographic and perception-related questions, achieving a high classification accuracy of 80%. This study is the first to simultaneously address perception, prediction, and uncertainty regarding COVID-19 preventive measures. It offers valuable insights for designing online campaigns and serves as a model for future research on public perceptions during pandemics. This investigation relies on examining stationary random walks on (normal) double cosets, specifically proving a mixing estimate for such walks when conducted on a fixed finite quotient. Notably, this approach diverges from Bass's characteristic polynomial method, which is inapplicable due to the groups' non-linearity. Furthermore, we establish a general criterion ensuring that a group $\G$ exhibits weak containment for its trivial representation relative to a finite quotient $\G/\!/\G'$, where $\G'$ possesses a small diameter. This criterion is derived from the asymptotic behavior of stationary random walks on finite quotients and has significant implications for the weak closure of the group algebra. In certain scenarios, this criterion also facilitates the demonstration of weak containment for the trivial representation via the characteristic polynomial method. As an application, we demonstrate that the weak containment result mentioned earlier implies a direct proof of Bass's criterion for normal subgroups of moderate dimension in arithmetic groups. Additionally, we examine the trivial representation and weak containment in quotient algebras specifically when the random walk is performed on a coset double coset. We establish a criterion ensuring mixing for such walks on a fixed finite quotient, thereby yielding a comprehensive list of arithmetic groups where the trivial representation is weakly contained relative to a cocompact cocommuting subgroup. Furthermore, we illustrate how this result enables the proof of the direct finiteness property for the group algebras of arithmetic groups when a commutative normal subgroup has a sufficiently small diameter. These findings are derived from a broader framework concerning the asymptotic behavior of stationary random walks on finite quotients of locally compact groups. This framework also elucidates the connections between weak containment, the property (T) for a group $\G$ relative to a subgroup $H$, and the dimension of $H$'s coset space. Specifically, we analyze two online strategies: the online maximum-entropy (OME) strategy and the sequential equal-likelihood (SE) strategy. We demonstrate that both strategies achieve optimal average success probabilities, with a ratio of $r_n$ between them as $n$ increases. We establish a lower bound of $r_n \geq 1 - \frac{1}{2}e^{-\frac{1}{4n}}$ for any $n$, proving that both strategies converge to optimality as $n \rightarrow \infty$. For the specific case of binary symmetric states, we prove that the success probabilities of both strategies are identical for all $n$, meaning both strategies are optimal in this context. Additionally, we extend our findings to online discrimination tasks involving symmetric states across an arbitrary finite-dimensional Hilbert space. We introduce a new strategy, the generalized equal-likelihood (GSE) strategy, which generalizes the SE strategy and demonstrates optimal average success probability. For this strategy, the gap between its average success probability and that of the optimal strategy is bounded by $\frac{1}{8n}$, confirming that the GSE strategy also becomes optimal as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Finally, we show that the optimal average success probability for discriminating symmetric states remains independent of the dimension of the full Hilbert space. These results rely on the asymptotic symmetry of the Kullback-Leibler divergence and the relative entropy of quantum states, with the latter playing a crucial role in the online discrimination of symmetric pure states. Our findings offer new insights into the theoretical framework of quantum state discrimination. Additionally, we present a general formula for the online discrimination of symmetric pure states and a specific formula for the sequential Bayesian discrimination of symmetric pure states, both of which may hold independent significance. The approach treats the electronic band structure of graphene as quantized while describing the electronic current as a classical continuous variable. Leveraging the unique electronic characteristics of graphene, this framework enables the investigation of electron transport under intense laser fields, including the generation of high-harmonic radiation. We demonstrate that the semi-classical model captures key phenomena such as the three-step model of a solid-state Landau-Zener (LZ) mechanism and the asymmetry in the electron wave packet within a driven double barrier structure. Furthermore, we show that this model simplifies the analysis of a particle in a double barrier as a quantum mechanics problem while incorporating the classical electron trajectory. Finally, we compare the findings from the semi-classical model with those from full time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations, which incorporate electron-electron interactions. The results indicate that the semi-classical model yields accurate predictions for the laser-induced electron current, power, and asymmetry of the wave packet in a driven double barrier, and the electronic transmission probability in a single barrier, relative to TDDFT results. Additionally, we observe that while the maximum values of these quantities match between the two models, the peak positions in the TDDFT results exhibit slight shifts due to electron-electron interactions. This research establishes a foundation for developing a comprehensive theory of laser-dressed electron transport in graphene, incorporating many-body effects. It also offers a robust tool for analyzing the quantum nature of laser-dressed electrons, with applications extending to the control of the asymmetry of the dressed electron wave packet and the generation of high-harmonic radiation in graphene. The proposed model is readily adaptable for studying laser-dressed electron transport in other two-dimensional materials exhibiting Dirac-like dispersion relations. This framework incorporates a type-II seesaw mechanism for neutrino masses alongside R-parity violation (RPV) for supersymmetry. We analyze RPV supersymmetry within this context, focusing on flavor physics constraints, particularly those arising from $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and neutrinoless double beta decay. Our results indicate that RPV scenarios are viable in the $\mu_2$-type benchmark but remain constrained in the $\mu_1$-type benchmark. Furthermore, we examine the phenomenology of rare $B$ meson decays and search signals at the LHC, with findings from these searches expected to offer significant insights into supersymmetric RPV models in the near future. Additionally, we investigate RPV scenarios that accommodate the recently reported $750\,\mathrm{GeV}$ resonance, discussing their implications for future $B$ meson decay measurements and LHC experiments. Finally, we explore the cosmological implications of these models, specifically regarding dark matter and baryogenesis. The supersymmetric $\mu_1$-type case predicts a gravitino dark matter candidate with masses ranging from approximately $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ to the supergravity scale, whereas the supersymmetric $\mu_2$-type scenario suggests a much heavier gravitino and an alternative dark matter candidate, the complex scalar field $S$, associated with $U(1)_X$. Furthermore, the supersymmetric $\mu_2$-type scenario offers a viable explanation for the baryon asymmetry of the universe through RPV leptogenesis. We also examine the "overdamping" problem for the gravitino in supersymmetric supergravity and propose a solution to mitigate this issue. Ultimately, we conclude that both the supersymmetric $\mu_1$-type and $\mu_2$-type scenarios remain promising and warrant further investigation. This work is dedicated to the memory of A. B. The system comprises $K$ information sources, an information destination, an energy source, and $N$ intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRSs), all of which harvest energy from the energy source via the same time slots. After harvesting, the destination utilizes the collected energy to transmit information, while the energy source remains silent. To maximize the destination's expected information rate, we jointly optimize the destination's transmit strategy and an IRS selection policy. Since the optimal solution is generally intractable, we first address the problem by assuming the destination has perfect channel state information (CSI) and power levels of direct links between transmitters and selected IRSs, proposing a suboptimal policy that achieves near-optimal performance. Subsequently, to reduce overhead, we investigate a robust design where the destination operates without perfect CSI, instead acquiring the CSI of the selected IRS. We demonstrate that the optimal policy remains unchanged despite the lack of perfect CSI at the transmitter, thereby minimizing performance loss. Finally, we evaluate the robustness of this policy against the use of approximate CSI at the selected IRS. Simulation results indicate that our proposed policies achieve performance within $1\%$ of the optimal case and remain robust against imperfect CSI at the selected IRS. Furthermore, our policies outperform benchmark approaches. These findings suggest that intelligent IRS selection can effectively mitigate wireless channel uncertainty. In this study, we performed a field trial of TF-QKD over 18.5 km of unspooled outdoor fiber under varying loss conditions. During the experiment, we experienced intermittent cloud cover that intermittently blocked the line of sight between the two endpoints. At a mean optical power of 10 dB, we achieved a secure key rate of 1.7 kbps, which remains consistent regardless of whether the outdoor link is blocked. We also analyzed the impact of polarization instability and observed a roughly 20% reduction in secure key rates due to the need for active compensation. These findings provide valuable insights for deploying non-hermitian QKD systems in outdoor fiber environments. Additionally, we demonstrated that employing a low-loss optical amplifier boosted the secure key rate by approximately 200%, highlighting the potential of hybrid fiber-free-freezer schemes for outdoor fiber applications. This work advances the practical implementation of QKD systems, particularly for hybrid architectures involving both indoor and outdoor fiber connections. Furthermore, the results support the exploration of quantum-enhanced applications beyond key distribution, such as quantum illumination and sensing, within outdoor fiber settings. Our findings contribute to the broader effort to refine the practical deployment of quantum technologies outside controlled laboratory settings. This star is situated at a distance of 0.13 pc from the center of the Rho Oph A dense core, which has an estimated visual extinction of 10 magnitudes. We propose that the dust surrounding S1 has been depleted through a "dust-eating" process, where the star's radiation pressure drives dust grains to collide and coalesce. This mechanism could account for the anomalous H2 column density, as well as the unusually low values for the 21 cm critical density parameter ($N_{\rm H_2}/I_{21{\rm cm}}$) and the total-to-selective extinction ratio ($R_V$) observed around S1. Additionally, this star may be responsible for the observed cavity in the surrounding molecular gas. The existence of such dust-depleted regions around other early-type stars in the Rho Oph region could be verified by measuring their H2 column densities and R_V values. If these stars also display depleted column densities and elevated R_V values, it would indicate that the effects are not unique to S1 but are part of a broader phenomenon. This process offers a novel explanation for the "blue hook" feature seen in the extinction versus wavelength relationship. Furthermore, if these effects are widespread, they could help resolve the long-standing discrepancy between the total mass calculated from the virial theorem and the sum of individual stellar masses in star clusters. Finally, this mechanism may contribute to the formation of massive stars, as stars with surrounding dust-depleted zones can accumulate more mass from the ambient medium. In this context, S1 might be a member of the Trumpler 14 variable-luminosity group. Ultimately, understanding and quantifying these effects is crucial for accurately interpreting the extinction versus wavelength relationship. A space is deemed to have a semistable fundamental group at infinity when, following quasi-isometry, it can be transformed into one where every element is homotopic to a sequence with a uniformly bounded number of non-trivial components, each possessing a lower bound on injectivity radius relative to the R-tree quasi-isometry quotient. Additionally, we outline quasilocal conditions that guarantee semistability. Specifically, for geodesically complete spaces, the stable subgroup property combined with the quasi-hyperbolic Bounded Coset Condition ensures that the fundamental group is semistable. We also analyze certain hyperbolic Coxeter groups, which are geodesically complete spaces sharing a common quasi-isometry quotient: a finite product of simplicial trees. Millions and Powerball draw significant public interest. However, these massive wins often trigger a surge in future participation, which negatively affects expected returns. This study examines the delay in interest response by modeling customer behavior as a function of both current and past jackpot sizes and recent draw results. Utilizing data from four major US lotteries over the last two decades, we developed a nonparametric model that captures this temporal lag more effectively than models ignoring such dynamics. Our estimation results indicate that customer response is delayed by approximately two to three weeks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this delayed response mechanism explains the observed decline in expected returns following a jackpot win. These findings offer valuable insights for designing optimal lottery products. Additionally, we provide R code implementing the proposed model, ensuring full reproducibility of our results. This work represents the first application of nonparametric estimation to estimate a delayed response function in a customer response model. It also represents an innovative method for analyzing time-varying customer behavior, distinct from traditional survival analysis. Finally, we illustrate how this response function can be integrated into lottery product design to enhance expected returns. We also explore the connection between this response function and price elasticity. Our code is available on GitHub. This review concentrates primarily on superfluid $^{4}$He and superconductors within the bosonic large-charge expansion framework, while also briefly addressing significant findings from other platforms. Superfluid $^{4}$He serves as the inaugural quantum many-body system where this approach proved effective; its primary objective is elucidating the collective excitation spectrum of the resulting superfluid. Similarly, in superconductors, the large-charge expansion aims to analyze the quasi-particle spectrum across various scales. This review comprehensively examines the methods employed to achieve these objectives, alongside numerous auxiliary topics including the large-charge expansion itself, Monte Carlo simulations, quantum Monte Carlo challenges, quasi-particle spectrum calculations, and the large-charge expansion's application to vortices, such as the statistics of vortex positions and the expansion's impact on the specific heat near the superconducting transition. Superconductivity near a Mott transition represents a particularly exciting regime for future large-charge expansion research. Furthermore, the method holds significant potential for strongly-coupled gauge theories, notably QCD, where it could facilitate the exploration of the spectrum at finite baryon density. Consequently, this review also delves into the implementation of large-charge expansion within QCD, including applications to the meson spectrum at finite density and the investigation of the sign problem in QCD. Additionally, this methodology may prove valuable for the nuclear many-body problem, especially in scenarios involving non-zero isospin asymmetry. Finally, the review briefly touches upon the large-charge expansion approach applied to the Skyrme model. Collectively, this review synthesizes the author's efforts spanning approximately the last decade, with a specific focus on bosonic large-charge expansion. It does not extensively cover fermionic large-charge expansion, which is addressed in a separate review by one of the authors. Finally, an extensive bibliography is provided, curated to be as comprehensive as possible. Although analog components are typically vulnerable to noise, rendering them incompatible with current reliable quantum information processing, we highlight a class of operations where analog mechanisms can be seamlessly integrated with hybrid digital-analog architectures. The core of our proposed algorithm involves reusing ancilla qubits to implement magic state injection through a specific protocol. This method leverages the partial computational information extracted from measurement-based stabilizer operations to facilitate ancilla qubit recovery. Theoretically, our approach can reduce the resource requirements of magic state injection by a factor of (1-p), where p represents the success probability of operations involving ancilla qubits. Consequently, this reduction translates to a significant decrease in computational resources, including the count of physical qubits, the duration of the injection process, and the number of injected instances. We anticipate that this strategy will be highly effective for quantum algorithms utilizing stabilizer-circuits, such as quantum phase estimation and quantum chemistry simulations. Additionally, this research holds substantial potential for optimizing the performance of future hybrid digital-analog quantum computers. This paper explores the most promising theoretical models capable of explaining this signal across multiple final states. We examine the phenomenology of a diquark $U_{\frac{5}{6}}$ within a grand unified framework that extends the minimal $SO(10)$ model by incorporating an additional $SU(5)$ gauge group. This specific model is motivated by its capacity to account for the LHC Higgs candidate, the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry, and neutrino oscillation data. We demonstrate that the model's primary representation, containing five right-handed quarks, two leptons, and an acronuclear diquark, naturally yields the correct baryon asymmetry and a satisfactory Higgs boson mass. Furthermore, the model offers a natural resolution to the smallness of neutrino masses and provides an explanation for the three generations of leptons and quarks. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for dark matter and for testing the model using a super-tau collider. We conclude that the Higgs boson candidate is likely explained by the Higgs boson of the minimal $SO(10)$ model, while the Higgs candidate $H_R$ can be probed at a Super-tau collider. Arabic to English frequently produce output riddled with spelling mistakes and grammatical errors. This issue stems from two main factors: the inherent difficulty Arabic presents for translation due to its complex morphology, and a limited capacity to learn from vast amounts of data. To address this, we introduce a post-editing method that enhances NMT translation quality by integrating an external Arabic Natural Language Generation (NLG) model. This hybrid approach combines the NMT translation model with the NLG model to refine translations. Our results demonstrate that this post-editing strategy improves the NMT translation quality by 1.06 points on the ROUGE-L metric. Additionally, we find that increasing the size of the training corpus further boosts the quality of the combined model. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of utilizing post-editing to enhance NMT translation quality through the integration of an NLG model. We also show that this technique can effectively improve other source languages when paired with appropriate NLG models. Experimental results indicate that the method yields the most significant improvements for languages possessing rich morphological structures, such as Arabic and Turkish. Finally, it is proven that the union of all regular conjugacy classes constitutes a union of orbits under the action of the Coxeter group generated by the simple reflections of $G$. The results are valid for $n > 2$ in types $B_n$ and $D_n$, and for $p > 1$ in type $A_{p+q+r}$. This study examines the transition between geostrophic and non-geostrophic regimes in rotating turbulent channel flow by systematically varying the rotation rate. The imposed rotation rate is notably higher than what is required to initiate Geostrophic Turbulence (GT) at high Reynolds numbers, a regime known as the Intermediate Rotation Rate (IRR) where GT and other balanced states coexist. This similarity suggests that both categories of stars utilize the plasma emission mechanism driven by electron cyclotron maser (ECM) instability. We propose that the onset of this frequency scaling regime in M dwarfs is also governed by the ratio of the electron cyclotron frequency to the plasma frequency. However, because the low-density regions responsible for ECM emission in M dwarfs are denser than those in solar type stars, the frequency regime begins at a lower value. This discrepancy in density conditions accounts for the observed variation in the magnetic field strengths required to trigger the cyclotron maser effect across different stellar types. Ultimately, the convergence of the frequency scaling regime in M dwarfs at lower frequencies is attributed to their higher atmospheric metallicities. These findings offer a pathway to determine the magnetic field strengths within the low-density regions of ECM-emitting stars. Furthermore, this proposed framework for the ECM onset in M dwarfs may also clarify the origins of the enigmatic "starquakes" detected in fast-rotating white dwarfs. In that context, the frequency scaling regime would be dictated by the cyclotron frequency of surface magnetic fields and the density of the white dwarf's atmosphere. Additionally, the rotation of the frequency scaling regime relative to the observer could explain the periodicity of spectral bursts from periodic X-ray transients, while the ECM onset could account for the observed magnetic field strengths in "starquaking" white dwarfs. Finally, we suggest that the ECM onset in white dwarfs could be modulated by stellar activity, such as mass accretion from a binary companion. These findings may also facilitate the discovery of new sources of coherent radio emission from white dwarfs and other white dwarf-like objects. spin-polarized variational Monte Carlo approach on the spin-$S=1/2$ Heisenberg-Ising model, which incorporates both nearest and next-nearest neighbor exchange interactions ($J_1$ and $J_2$) alongside an external magnetic field. Our analysis identifies two distinct regimes: a quasi-one-dimensional regime, where magnetic properties are governed by the competition between $J_1$, $J_2$, and the external field, and a three-dimensional regime, where the stronger external field suppresses quasi-1D behavior, resulting in an isotropic Heisenberg system. Our study successfully maps out the magnetic phase diagram across a wide range of temperatures and establishes the phase boundaries. Furthermore, we examine the critical exponents and scaling functions for the quasi-1D regime, demonstrating that the system exhibits 3D Heisenberg universality. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results in relation to the 2008 observation of an exotic, highly frustrated, and highly conductive spin liquid phase in the organic conductor $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$CuBr$_4$. This phase displays significant 3D Heisenberg universality despite occurring in a 2D system, a characteristic that remains difficult to explain using conventional symmetry-breaking order parameters. Our simulations suggest that this apparent paradox can be resolved by considering strong electron-electron correlations. Additionally, we show that the observed universality is not contingent upon the specific crystallographic orientation of the external magnetic field. These findings are supported by an analysis of the dynamic spin structure factor and its associated scaling functions. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of non-integer filling on the phase diagram, revealing that it can induce a transition from a dimerized to a valence bond crystal phase. observable consequences of a recently proposed dark matter candidate: the lightest non-thermal fermion arising from a U(1)$_X$ extension of the Standard Model. We analyze its production mechanisms within the Standard Model effective theory and study potential signals at the Large Hadron Collider. Specifically, we demonstrate that for dark matter masses below approximately 5 GeV, experimental production cross sections are notably suppressed, rendering LHC detection unfeasible. However, in the mass range of 5 to 10 GeV, we identify a substantial portion of the parameter space that remains accessible. Future facilities, including the High-Luminosity LHC and electron-positron colliders, will offer significantly improved sensitivity to this region. Additionally, we examine the dark matter production timeline and constraints imposed by cosmic microlensing observations. Our findings indicate that dark matter within this mass window would have formed shortly after the Big Bang, and we show that microlensing data do not restrict the viable parameter space. Overall, we conclude that Lichtenberg's dark matter candidate remains a compelling target for future collider research. Furthermore, we suggest that upcoming precision experiments at the LHC and CE$\nu$BB will enable a more rigorous exploration of the parameter space predicted to exist in the early Universe. Finally, we address the issue of fine-tuning in this model, noting that while the smallness of the electron mass presents a challenge, it is not particularly problematic. We also argue that the model does not suffer from excessive fine-tuning regarding the dark matter mass itself. In summary, we contend that Lichtenberg's proposal merits further investigation regarding both its theoretical consistency and experimental testability. We believe that future studies should address the fine-tuning inherent in the model and utilize future collider experiments to test the associated parameter space. Such efforts will provide a definitive assessment of the model's testability and potential viability. \textbf{Keywords:} Dark Matter, U(1)$_X$, Lichtenberg Model, LHC, CE$\nu$BB, Fine-Tuning. \textbf{PACS numbers:} 95.35.Dc, 14.60.Pt, 12.60.-i, 13.40.Ev, 14.60.St. \textbf{PACS numbers:} 95.35.Dc, 14.60.Pt, 12.60.-i, 13.40.Ev, 1

investigate the low-temperature characteristics of the one-dimensional Heisenberg-Ising model under a transverse magnetic field within an infinite dimerized zigzag chain, focusing on two spin excitations with alternating quasimomenta. Our analysis examines their temperature-dependent quasiparticle quasimotions and the associated dynamical structure factor. We observe that at the model's ground state, spin excitations manifest as either right- or left-moving waves, contingent upon the magnetic field's magnitude. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the dynamical structure factor reaches its peak when the spin excitation moves in the direction opposite to the momentum of the quasiparticle. These results provide significant insights into the dynamical behavior of spin excitations in the model's low-temperature regime. Finally, we propose that this method could serve as a valuable tool for studying spin excitations in the experimentally realized quasicrystalline Kitaev quantum spin liquid compound $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the dynamical structure factor can be interpreted as a manifestation of the Fermi surface in the quasiparticle quasimotion diagram. This interpretation offers a pathway to extend our methodology to more complex quasicrystalline models. Our results also suggest that the concept of a Fermi surface in low-temperature quasiparticle quasimotions should be broadened to encompass quasicrystalline models. In conclusion, our study provides a novel perspective on the dynamical behavior of spin excitations as quasicrystalline analogues of spin liquids. By employing the tensor network density-matrix renormalization group method, we numerically computed the dynamical structure factor for two spin excitations possessing opposite quasimomenta in the one-dimensional Heisenberg-Ising model (including next-nearest-neighbor interactions) situated within an infinite dimerized zigzag chain. Our focus centers on the temperature-dependent dynamical structure factor at the quantum critical point of the quasiparticle quasimotion diagram, where spin excitations exhibit opposite quasimotions relative to their quasiparticle quasimomenta. the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method is widely used. However, the standard DSMC approach introduces significant numerical errors in rarefied conditions, particularly in continuum regions. This paper introduces a novel numerical flux approach that enhances DSMC accuracy within continuum domains by calculating mass fluxes at cell interfaces. This is achieved by mapping the macroscopic flux derived from the kinetic solution in the DSMC cell adjacent to the continuum domain onto the continuum boundary. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme reduces numerical errors, effectively recovering the solution of the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations in continuum neighborhoods. Crucially, this improvement does not compromise DSMC's inherent accuracy within rarefied domains. Numerical tests confirm the scheme's efficacy across a wide range of rarefaction regimes. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of computational cost shows that the new approach requires at most a 10% increase in CPU time compared to the standard DSMC method. Finally, the scheme's robustness is verified through applications to complex geometries and a shock tube scenario. These findings indicate that the proposed method holds great promise for accurately simulating rarefied gas flows. Keywords: Direct simulation Monte Carlo numerical flux, accurate mapping.

To achieve this, the EIC will operate in an electron-nucleus or electron-nucleus beam configuration. An innovative technique for detecting photon-photon interactions involves the production of open-flavor meson pairs. This study examines the potential for observing such photon-photon interactions at the EIC through the creation of $D\bar{D}$ pairs, specifically focusing on the leptonic decay of charm hadrons. To evaluate the feasibility of this method across various experimental setups, we have conducted simulations for $e^+e^-\rightarrow Z^0/\gamma\gamma\rightarrow D\bar{D}+X$ events at a center-of-mass energy of 455 GeV. These findings suggest that measuring photon-photon interactions at the EIC is achievable, even under challenging conditions. as "quasi-periodic oscillations" (QPOs) in the M87 black hole, researchers have identified a second instance of this phenomenon in the nearby galaxy 3C 295. This discovery is particularly significant for 3C 295 because it is a well-studied radio galaxy that has served as a benchmark for testing various models of the X-ray emission from M87. The study, conducted using the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE), involved observations over a period of 1,000 days and utilized the satellite's Proportional Counter Array (PCA) to detect the oscillation in 3C 295. The analysis involved dividing the data into segments of approximately 300 days and searching for power in the 0.1 to 10 Hz frequency range. Power was identified in the 0.1 to 0.3 Hz band during two specific periods: between days 1,000 and 1,200, and between days 1,500 and 1,800. The peak power frequency within this range was estimated at 0.14 Hz. The amplitude of the oscillation was calculated by determining the fractional variation in flux between the peaks and troughs of the waveforms, resulting in an amplitude of roughly 0.15. These findings indicate that the variability observed in 3C 295 is consistent with the QPOs previously detected in M87. This detection represents the first instance of a QPO being observed in a nearby galaxy and the second such occurrence within the M87 cluster. The authors suggest that the origin of these QPOs may be linked to the magnetohydrodynamic activity of an accretion disk surrounding the central black hole. Furthermore, the authors note that the lack of QPO detection in other radio galaxies, such as Centaurus A, could be attributed to the higher mass of their black holes. The results also imply that the mechanisms generating QPOs in M87 and 3C 295 are likely similar. Additionally, the authors discuss the potential for future research to explore the relationship between QPOs and the physical properties of the source, including black hole mass and accretion rate. Finally, the authors conclude that the detection of QPOs in 3C 295 is a crucial finding that will significantly advance our understanding of the physical processes occurring in the centers of active galaxies

The data were analyzed using a model that simulates the vertical distribution of gas and dust. The observations reveal a depletion of CO in the disk's upper atmosphere, a finding consistent with CO being sequestered as CO$_2$. This gas-phase CO$_2$ is expected to condense into dust particles, which then migrate inward via radial drift, thereby lowering CO$_2$ concentrations in the disk's inner regions. Finally, the study confirms that the disk's surface temperature is approximately 100 K, a value that remains consistent with other temperature indicators. mode-locked oscillators are essential for research and applications spanning spectroscopy, nonlinear physics, and laser chemistry. This review examines the primary techniques for shaping these pulses, including spatial and temporal modulation within the intracavity dispersion region, spectral filtering using a spatial light modulator, and shaping via a liquid crystal spatial light modulator in the intracavity beam path. The most effective approach combines a Gaussian temporal modulation shape with a Gaussian spectral filter shape; this method is fully reflective, allows for rapid pulse-to-pulse modulation, and can handle intracavity modulator amplitudes up to 100 kW. Furthermore, spectral modulation can be applied to the fundamental longitudinal mode without affecting higher-order modes. By integrating all shaping techniques, it is possible to generate microsecond-long pulses with sub-10-fs time-bandwidth products. These tailored pulses find diverse applications, such as enhancing Raman spectroscopy sensitivity through spectral filtering, utilizing modulated intracavity intensity for optical Kerr gating, employing modulated spectral amplitude for four-wave mixing, and leveraging spatially modulated intracavity intensity and phase for optical Kerr-lens spectroscopy. Additionally, free-induction decay signals can be recorded using a modulated intracavity intensity profile. In conclusion, the capabilities for intracavity pulse shaping have expanded significantly, and ongoing research continues to refine these techniques. Intracavity pulse shaping serves as a powerful intrapulse cross-correlation technique, offering high efficiency and stability. Moreover, intracavity shaping can be integrated with various pulse-compression methods to generate long pulses with a sub-10-fs time-bandwidth product. These techniques are also applicable to other Kerr-lens mode-locked lasers, such as Ti:sapphire and Cr:ZnS oscillators. Finally, intracavity pulse shaping is a valuable tool for generating optical solitons. In both scenarios, we identify two optimal driving intensities that maximize the average shortening time for the oscillator's trajectory. Within the potential well, these intensity limits are determined by the convergence of oscillator trajectories to a stable attractor and by the slip of the oscillation frequency away from the slipless frequency. In contrast, for double-well potentials, the lower bound is established by slip-stick motion, whereas the upper bound arises from the double-well's symmetry. Our findings indicate that the intensity of the multiplicative noise significantly influences the average shortening time of the oscillator's trajectory, a phenomenon that would not occur with additive noise. This study underscores the critical role of intensity-dependent characteristics in slip-stick phenomena and marks a novel advancement in the investigation of convergence to attractors and path shortening within multiplicative noise environments. Ultimately, our results may offer valuable insights for designing and managing systems operating under slip-stick conditions. While many existing methods rely on the assumption that data resides on low-dimensional subspaces, this assumption is often too rigid for practical use. This paper addresses the challenge of recovering a rank-$r$ matrix from linear measurements of line integrals, where data points are assumed to lie on a union of a small number of low-dimensional subspaces. We introduce a weighted $l_1$-regularized estimator and establish non-asymptotic bounds for its estimation error under the condition that the rank and the count of subspaces are known. Subsequently, we extend these findings to a scenario where the rank and the number of subspaces must be determined simultaneously. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments. Our contributions are threefold: (i) We resolve the weighted estimator formulation within the generalized total variation regularizer framework. (ii) We derive non-asymptotic error bounds for the estimator under conditions requiring only that data lies on a union of low-dimensional subspaces. (iii) We provide theoretical support for model selection procedures. Our proposed methodology and error bounds are distinct from existing techniques and results. Furthermore, our numerical comparisons demonstrate that the weighted estimator outperforms the unweighted version. Utilizing the classical spectrum as a foundation for an effective low-energy quantum spectrum, we examine how nonlinear self-interaction impacts Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC). Our analysis reveals that nonlinear self-interaction can either suppress or enhance BEC, contingent upon the specific model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that BEC in this system can be understood through the lens of Anderson pseudospins. In regimes characterized by strong nonlinear self-interaction, these spins exhibit a ferromagnetic state, which corresponds to the complete disappearance of BEC. Conversely, in weakly interacting systems, the spins form a spin liquid phase, indicating that BEC remains enhanced. Additionally, we explore the impact of nonlinear self-interaction on spin waves propagating within the system. We find that nonlinear self-interaction causes significant stretching of spin wave wavelengths, leading to substantial red shifts in the vibrational spectrum. These findings are supported by both Monte Carlo simulations and analytical calculations. Overall, nonlinear self-interaction offers a powerful mechanism for manipulating vibrational modes in both classical and quantum moiré systems. Our theoretical framework and predictions can be experimentally validated through studies on Floquet-Bose-Hubbard models and other nonlinear self-interacting moiré materials. Moreover, these results offer a pathway to achieving long-range order in 1D quantum systems. By integrating various decay channels, $R_\Sigma$ offers enhanced sensitivity to Wilson coefficients compared to traditional measurements. Furthermore, we propose a corresponding ratio for the rare decay $K^+\to \pi^+\pi^0\mu^+\mu^-$ to facilitate future muon-to-positron conversion experiments. Our proposed measurements at Belle II and the NA62 experiment could achieve sensitivities of approximately $10^{-3}$ and roughly $10^{-2}$, respectively. These results would enable the detection of Wilson coefficient deviations as small as $10^{-3}$, corresponding to $\mathcal{O}(10^{-14})$ sensitivity in $\mu\to e\gamma$ searches. Additionally, we identify a potential $\mu/e$ universality test in the well-measured $D_s\to K^+\pi^+\pi^0$ channel, which is already accessible at the Fermilab SeaBeam facility. This analysis can be extended to other hadronic processes, including $B$-mesons, to explore new physics. Ultimately, these measurements provide a robust test of the Standard Model and a pathway to investigate new physics scenarios. Furthermore, we note that $R_\Sigma$ is sensitive to interference effects between tree-level and loop-level amplitudes, a feature that can induce deviations from the naive parton model expectation. This characteristic is also observed in other processes, such as the rare decay $B_c\to J/\psi K^+\pi^+\pi^0$. Consequently, $R_\Sigma$ serves as a valuable probe for the interplay between tree-level and loop-level contributions in hadronic processes. Finally, we have conducted a comprehensive study of the production cross-section for $R_\Sigma$ at the Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee) and the Circular $e^+e^-\mu^- \mu^+$ collider (CEEC), evaluating the potential for these facilities to test the $\mu/e$ universality of Wilson coefficients. The results indicate that $R_\Sigma$ measurements at the FCC-ee and CEEC can achieve sensitivities of approximately $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-2}$, respectively. eco-evolution) has gained significant traction in ecology and evolution, driven by the need to model complex interactions between ecological and evolutionary processes. In this domain, evolutionary changes are typically assumed to occur on a timescale that is either much faster or much slower than ecological processes. This assumption is justified by the fact that evolving species often coexist with others that are effectively asexual and thus asexual.

However, the dynamics of ecosystems populated exclusively by sexual species have received comparatively less attention. This paper introduces a novel field of study: the simultaneous dynamics of three asexual and two sexual species. We demonstrate that the system comprising five asexual species is governed by a linear map, whereas the dynamics of the four sexual species follow a more complex, non-linear trajectory. Consequently, we establish sufficient conditions for the local asymptotic stability of both the eco-evolutionary system and the equilibrium points of the four sexual species. Furthermore, numerical simulations are presented to illustrate these findings. Ultimately, this work offers a new perspective on sexual ecosystem dynamics, opening avenues for future research.

This study examines several existing approaches and introduces a novel method designed to assess how input parameter uncertainty affects model performance. This new framework is termed the General Fuzzy Sensitivity Analysis (GFSA). A primary objective is to quantify model performance in the presence of uncertain input parameters, which is particularly critical when modeling complex systems. The proposed method employs concepts from Possibility Theory and Fuzzy Set Theory to represent model performance under conditions of uncertainty. The study outlines the procedural steps for applying GFSA to performance evaluation and provides a practical application involving the analysis of a groundwater basin's response to varying parameter inputs. In this context, the model's performance is represented as a General Fuzzy Number, enabling the visualization of model performance as the input parameters change. The results indicate that performance is generally low when inputs are constant, rises when at least one input varies, and reaches its maximum when two or more inputs vary simultaneously. This confirms GFSA's efficacy in quantizing model performance in relation to the degree of variability among model input parameters. Furthermore, the study demonstrates how to determine optimal parameter combinations to maximize model performance. The General Fuzzy Set offers an effective means of capturing fuzziness arising from uncertainty in model inputs, facilitating the calculation of the optimal set of parameters that yield the best model performance. Additionally, a Defuzzification technique is introduced to convert the General Fuzzy Set into a crisp set, thereby providing a precise value for the optimal model performance. The findings from the Groundwater Basin application illustrate how GFSA can effectively evaluate model performance given the variability of model input parameters. The study concludes that the GFSA framework is suitable for performance evaluation when model input parameters are uncertain. The paper also includes a discussion on the advantages and limitations of the proposed approach. Overall, this research aims to advance Sensitivity Analysis methods and offer new perspectives for future studies. GFSA offers a means to quantify model performance while accounting for uncertainty in model input parameters. The study demonstrates that utilizing a General Fuzzy Set to represent model input parameters is an effective strategy for sensitivity analysis, as it accounts for the fuzziness introduced by uncertainty. Finally, a defuzzification method is introduced to convert the General Fuzzy Set into a crisp set, yielding a precise value for optimal model performance. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has significantly advanced the field of autonomous driving, the resulting policies often struggle to generalize when encountering unseen scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that integrates two recent advancements: (1) a new algorithm for generating and solving constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) and (2) the principles of few-shot learning. Our method, named Few-Shot Reinforcement Learning via Constraint Solving (FSRL-CS), aims to develop policies capable of predicting actions for previously unseen driving scenarios by leveraging a minimal number of examples. By utilizing the few-shot learning capabilities of qsarlnn and its ability to produce constraint solutions, we demonstrate that our approach can effectively handle unseen scenarios. Furthermore, we show that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in predicting actions for these unseen situations. Finally, we evaluate the method's performance on the CARLA simulator and the NAVE driving benchmark. The results indicate that our approach outperforms baseline methods in the critical task of predicting actions for unseen scenarios. Additionally, the method exhibits superior generalization, maintaining robust performance even when navigating scenarios that differ substantially from the training data. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Fsrl_cs. The associated paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.07505.

We demonstrate that the resulting utility function is not only equivalent to the original decision function but also possesses a closed-form expression. This study serves as a sequel to our previous research (Park & Rhee, 2019), where the two-point logistic function was first introduced to solve the inverse problem for logit utility functions. In that prior work, we proved the analytical equivalence between utility and decision functions under the condition that the decision function adheres to an additive form with a constant slope. The methodology in that paper was not applicable to decision functions outside this additive framework; however, the current study confirms the equivalence between utility and decision functions for all consistent, risk-averse, and quasi-concave decision functions. Additionally, the inverse problem for decision functions within this class can be solved directly via algebraic calculation, whereas the approach in our previous paper relied on numerical methods. This paper introduces an alternative algebraic solution, which is more efficient than the procedure employed in our earlier work. The derived utility function is analytically expressed using elementary functions and the two-point logistic function. This utility function is particularly valuable for applications involving multi-response data, including ordinal regression, ranking, and preference analysis. It effectively models phenomena characterized by a natural upper bound, a lack of symmetry, and a steep increase followed by a gradual decline. Notably, this two-point logistic function is not limited to continuous variables but is also applicable to discrete variables. Consequently, this utility function is highly effective for modeling phenomena exhibiting a discrete nature. The study concludes with an application to the ordinal regression task. A prevalent strategy involves defining an objective function to quantify the discrepancy between model predictions and observations, which is then minimized using stochastic algorithms. This paper examines how measurement noise and missing data influence the variance of these algorithms specifically when applied to the Stokes equations. We analyze scenarios where both the gradient field and the vector field are observed, demonstrating that the vector field's gradient drives the variance of the optimization process. Furthermore, we establish that the variance is optimally minimized when observations are collected along specific manifolds, a result applicable to both gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. These findings are derived through a stochastic analysis of a continuum model, where the objective function represents the model-data mismatch and the state variable acts as a regularization term. This continuum model emerges from the discrete objective function used in computational fluid dynamics. Additionally, we present numerical experiments that validate our theoretical predictions and contrast the variances of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. Our continuous framework offers a novel approach for quantifying uncertainty in inverse problems within computational fluid dynamics. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundation for extending the analysis to more intricate cases involving nonlinear equations and ill-posed inverse problems. Initially, we derive a system of necessary conditions for optimality applicable to problems with a single control variable, which subsequently serves as a foundation for addressing problems involving multiple control variables. Our findings indicate that this method is effective for solving optimal control problems involving time delays and multiple control variables. By utilizing a differentiable, non-linear optimization technique, our approach leverages features extracted by a vision transformer and the geometric constraints provided by a volumetric scene representation to produce pose estimates that are consistent with scene geometry. Compared to traditional neural network methods, our framework is more resilient to out-of-distribution inputs, such as unfamiliar objects and extreme poses, because the scene representation helps mitigate these challenges. However, because data quality is fundamental to model performance, existing research has largely overlooked how quality issues in training and testing data impact the explainability of global models. This study empirically examines the effects of two common data quality problems—class imbalance and missing values—on explainable deep learning models. Our findings indicate that class imbalance negatively affects feature importance and decision path explanations, whereas missing values have minimal impact. are extensively utilized in quantum information science for developing topological qubits and sensing applications. This study examines how random coupling to environmental degrees of freedom affects these systems. Specifically, we analyze the impact of disorder on the conductance of a topological superconducting nanowire connected to superconducting reservoirs. We compare two scenarios: one where the nanowire is fabricated separately and subsequently wired to the reservoirs, and another where all components are created as a single integrated system. Our results indicate that in the integrated system, a significant portion of the nanowire's conductance remains robust against coupling to environmental noise. This resilience stems from the self-averaging nature of the superconducting quantum coherence within the system. Conversely, the nanowire fabricated separately is highly sensitive to such coupling, leading to a substantial decrease in conductance. These findings offer critical insights into the architecture of topological devices, suggesting that to preserve the delicate topological properties, components should be integrated to minimize interactions with the external environment. Furthermore, our results suggest that the recently observed conductance plateau in experimental setups can be accounted for by the disorder-induced self-averaging of the superconducting order parameter. This mechanism effectively filters out incoherent quasiparticle transport from the nanowire, leaving the coherent contribution from Majorana modes as the dominant factor. Consequently, this phenomenon offers a novel pathway to mitigate noise in devices utilizing superconducting quantum coherence. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the design of topological devices. We demonstrate that a simple design modification—connecting the nanowire to the ground through a normal metal wire—can enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of the measured conductance. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending these results to other devices that rely on superconducting quantum coherence. Our analysis is based on a combination of analytical methods and numerical simulations. The numerical approach employs a real-space Green's function technique to model a mesoscopic network consisting of a nanowire linked to normal and superconducting metallic leads. To self-consistently solve the resulting self-consistent Born approximation equations, we utilize a recently developed numerical algorithm. We also provide a comprehensive discussion of the assumptions and approximations used, ensuring that our conclusions remain valid within the parameter ranges established by current state-of-the-art experiments. This paper applies that formalism to a specific class of symmetric metric-affine theories characterized by a scalar field theory Lagrangian and utilizing the Cartan decomposition to resolve the field equations. The resulting metric equations mirror those of general relativity, with the Einstein-Hilbert action augmented by terms that are homogeneous of degree one in curvature and possess a structure analogous to the Chern-Simons form. We explicitly construct the observability four-forms and demonstrate that, despite their general complexity, they simplify to expressions similar to those in general relativity when evaluated on-shell. Furthermore, we derive the field equations and solutions for a cosmological model based on this formalism, where the Gourdeau et al. (2019) observability four-forms generate an effective energy-momentum tensor. This approach yields an exact analytic solution to the cosmological field equations, the form of which depends on the specific choice of Lagrangian. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for the acceleration of the Universe's expansion. We show that even without a cosmological constant, an appropriately chosen metric-affine Lagrangian can enable the transition from decelerated to accelerated expansion at the current epoch. Additionally, we note that the metric-affine Lagrangian can be interpreted as an effective dark energy model. Our results indicate that this Lagrangian exhibits curvature-dependent behavior, transitioning from an Einstein-de Sitter form at low curvatures to a de Sitter form at high curvatures. This represents the first such solution derived from a metric-affine theory. The findings are discussed in the context of current observational data. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the richness of the metric-affine theory framework and its strong potential for addressing current challenges in cosmology. (Abridged)
